item.title: Flying Elephants
item.description: Why science requires more than an elegant hypothesis. The role of photographs, videos, specimens, and primary data in building and verifying scientific conclusions.

item.title: What Is Your Evidence?
item.description: Why photographs, videos, and polished explanations are no longer enough in the age of generative AI. A practical look at provenance, documentation, and trust in scientific evidence.

item.title: Fossa Method
item.description: Observation, constraints, models, understanding, and the search for mechanisms. A collection of principles that gradually emerged from diagnostics, research, and everyday problem-solving.

item.title: Scientific Method. A Practical Guide.
item.description: How knowledge is formed, why confidence often outpaces understanding, and how the scientific method helps distinguish observation from interpretation.

item.title: Tradition Instead of Science I. Method
item.description: What can staining reveal when the classical Ziehl–Neelsen method cannot be performed in full? We examine the roles of phenol, heating and acid decolorization, and learn to distinguish observations from what the method actually demonstrates.

item.title: Traditions Instead of Science. II
item.description: Why a familiar treatment protocol does not automatically become evidence-based therapy. Using FMC as an example, we examine how concentration, exposure time, the suspected pathogen, and the condition of the fish determine whether a treatment makes sense.

item.title: Traditions Instead of Science. III
item.description: A fish rubs against the substrate — but is it really “itching,” let alone “scratching its gills”? We examine where observation ends and interpretation of behavior begins.

item.title: Traditions Instead of Science IV. Diagnosis.
item.description: Granulomas, necrosis, and mycobacteriosis in fish: why similar morphological findings do not imply the same etiology and cannot, on their own, establish a diagnosis.

item.title: Granulomas in Fish: What Their Structure Reveals—and What It Cannot Prove
item.description: Granulomatous reactions, mycobacteriosis, and differential diagnosis: how to distinguish a morphological finding from the cause of a lesion.

item.title: Phenol-Free Staining: What Changes in the Method and the Conclusions
item.description: Why omitting phenol does not necessarily prevent bacteria from being detected, while skipping acid decolorization changes the diagnostic question itself.

item.title: Red Rods: Why I Changed the Usual Method
item.description: How three staining methods applied to samples from the same angelfish spleen helped reveal bacteria—and why seeing them is not the same as making a diagnosis.

item.title: White Spots in Fish Organs: Is It Tuberculosis?
item.description: Two fish spleens have similar-looking white nodules. Why appearance alone cannot tell us whether mycobacteria are responsible.

item.title: FMC: Why a Treatment Bath Is Not the Same as Effective Treatment
item.description: An examination of FMC use in fish: mixture composition, historical treatment regimens, concentration and exposure time, parasite susceptibility, and the limits of claims about efficacy.

item.title: We Gave the Fish a Bath. But Did We Cure It?
item.description: Why ten minutes in a medicated bath does not necessarily mean a fish has recovered. A simple story about FMC, parasites, and the habit of treating fish by following a routine.

item.title: Fish Rubbing Against Objects: Behavior, Cause, and Diagnosis
item.description: Why flashing alone cannot distinguish skin irritation, gill disease, and other possible causes. Observation, interpretation, and hypothesis testing.

item.title: The Fish Is Scratching. But Why?
item.description: A fish rubs against rocks — does that mean it has parasites? Why a single movement cannot tell us what is happening to its skin or gills.

item.title: Twigs and Rods. Can We Identify Bacteria by Their Shape?
item.description: Red rods in a fish specimen: why they are not necessarily mycobacteria, how dangerous nocardiosis can be, and why staining cannot guide treatment on its own.

item.title: Twigs and Rods. What Can Shape and Staining Tell Us?
item.description: Nocardia and Mycobacterium in fish: morphology, pathogenicity, partial acid-fastness, and antimicrobial susceptibility.

item.title: Twigs and Rods. Who Are We Looking at in This Specimen?
item.description: Nocardia and Mycobacterium in fish: comparing morphology, acid-fastness, pathogenicity, and antibiotic resistance, and understanding the limits of diagnosis.

item.title: Virtual Microscope — Wide View
item.description: Explore FossaMethod's interactive microscopy slides in a wide two-panel interface with Deep Zoom and annotations.

item.title: Fin Damage: Erosion, Infection, and Fin-Ray Structure
item.description: Why similarly frayed fins may have different causes: the structure of lepidotrichia, non-infectious erosion, columnaris disease, and the role of microscopy.

item.title: Frayed Fins. Who's to Blame?
item.description: A fish's fins are breaking down. Does that mean bacterial fin rot? A simple demonstration with a fin ray shows why appearance alone cannot reveal the cause.

item.title: Health Does Not Mean Sterility
item.description: Why the presence of microorganisms and parasites does not always mean disease, why immunity does not have to eliminate them completely, and why the use of medications requires an assessment of the animal, the environment, and the consequences of intervention.

item.title: Cryptocaryonosis: killing the parasite or treating the water?
item.description: A practical analysis of cryptocaryonosis treatment in marine fish: why killing the parasite should not become more important than the condition of the fish itself, how to reduce the parasite burden quickly, and how to limit reinfection.

item.title: Publications
item.description: Scientific articles, conference materials, and supplementary resources on fish pathology, fish disease diagnostics, and aquarium systems.

item.title: Gas Bubble Disease. Part II. Consequences.
item.description: Comparison of normal and pathological findings in fish necropsy: liver, kidney, gills, and brain. How to distinguish acceptable variation from signs of congestion, tissue damage, and hypoxia.

item.title: Fish coccidia: Goussia
item.description: Coccidia of the genus Goussia in fish. Morphology of oocysts, sporocysts, and sporozoites, with diagnostic interpretation of microscopic findings.

item.title: Cryptococcus-like structures in fish
item.description: Round structures with a distinct halo, morphologically resembling cryptococci. Morphological analysis and limitations of interpretation.

item.title: Fungal structures in fish: colonization or invasive process
item.description: Fungal structures in fish may represent either surface colonization or an invasive process. This article discusses morphological features, localization, and diagnostic interpretation.

item.title: Granulomatous lesions in fish: a histoplasma-like case
item.description: Granulomas in fish kidneys and spleen with negative results for mycobacteria. Detection of intracellular yeast-like organisms and differential interpretation.

item.title: Granulomas and intracellular agents in fish
item.description: A collection of real observations: intracellular yeast-like organisms, coccidia, cryptosporidia, and fungal structures in fish.

item.title: Fin Rot
item.description: Fin damage in fish is not always caused by bacterial infection. Lepidotrichial structure, noninfectious fin erosion, columnaris disease, and the limits of diagnosis.

item.title: Hexamitids Without Myths
item.description: Why hexamitids are not a normal component of fish intestinal microflora, where the myth of 'internal parasites' comes from, and how intestinal pathology actually develops.

item.title: Ichthyophthiriosis Without Myths
item.description: A science-based analysis of Ichthyophthirius multifiliis: life cycle, cyst terminology, the myth of parasite ubiquity, and real mechanisms of transmission.

item.title: Patient Size Doesn’t Matter — Why Fish Don’t Die From Diagnostics
item.description: Debunking the myth that diagnostic procedures kill fish. Non-lethal examination techniques, compensatory physiology, and why mortality sometimes follows handling.

item.title: Simple Rules for Working with Aquarium Fish
item.description: Basic guidelines for diagnosing and caring for aquarium fish: what to do in case of mortality, how to interpret appetite, and when to treat bacterial infections.

item.title: Surgical Procedures on Aquatic Animals
item.description: A Guide on performing surgical procedures on fish.

item.title: Is It Ever Too Late for a Fish Autopsy?
item.description: Debunking the myth: why you can examine a fish hours after death—not just in the first 30 minutes.

item.title: Two Sides of One Dosage
item.description: Aquarium medications: remedy or threat? Pros and cons of antibiotics, formalin, methylene blue, malachite green, and the FMC mixture.

item.title: Initial Diagnostics After Fish Transportation
item.description: Microscopy, smears, staining methods, and common mistakes in early diagnostics.

item.title: Gas Bubble Disease: It's Not About the Bubbles
item.description: Gas Bubble Disease in fish is not caused by air bubbles entering the gills but by dissolved gas supersaturation. This article explains the true mechanism, common misconceptions, and how to prevent the condition.

item.title: The Smear Comes First.
item.description: A reflection on why smear microscopy often matters more than bacterial culture in fish pathology. Real cases, logic, and the danger of trusting paperwork over tissue.

item.title: Cryptocaryon irritans: Not Just White Spots
item.description: Cryptocaryon irritans. is a ciliated protozoan parasite, often visible to the naked eye. Tangs, butterflyfish, and boxfish are particularly susceptible and typically among the first to become infected. The free-swimming infectious stage — theront — most often attaches to gills and fins. That’s why these areas should always be examined first

item.title: Black beard algae
item.description: Red algae commonly found on aquarium plants...

item.title: Black brush algae (presumably Audouinella) — 10×
item.description: General view of the bush-like thallus of a red alga, provisionally identified as Audouinella sp. The attachment region with rhizoids is visible at the top of the image. Zooming in reveals branching cellular filaments, transverse septa, and putative monosporangia.

item.title: Black brush algae (presumably Audouinella) — 20×
item.description: A branching network of multicellular filaments. The branching pattern, cellular segmentation, and rounded reproductive structures on short lateral branches are clearly visible.

item.title: Black brush algae (presumably Audouinella) — 40×
item.description: Detailed structure of the branching filaments of a red alga. Individual cells, transverse septa, and rounded structures on lateral branches, presumably monosporangia, are clearly visible.

item.title: Bolbitis fern — leaf cells, 40×
item.description: Leaf blade fragment of Bolbitis sp. Transmitted light, 40× objective. Cell outlines, numerous green structures presumed to be chloroplasts, and branching regions of leaf venation are visible.

item.title: Bolbitis fern — leaf, 10×
item.description: Leaf blade fragment of Bolbitis sp. Transmitted light, 10× objective. Vein regions and a mosaic-like tissue pattern with polygonal cell outlines are visible.

item.title: Branching filamentous bacteria — 100×
item.description: Spleen impression smear. Ziehl–Neelsen staining. 100× objective. Fuchsin-positive rod-shaped and filamentous structures showing prominent branching and uneven staining. The morphology is suggestive of branching actinomycetes, including Nocardia.

item.title: Branching rod-shaped bacteria — 40×
item.description: Spleen impression smear. Ziehl–Neelsen staining. 40× objective. Fuchsin-positive rod-shaped and elongated structures showing apparent branching. The morphology is compatible with Nocardia or other actinomycetes.

item.title: Bubble formation
item.description: 3D visualization of bubble formation in supersaturated water.

item.title: Capsalid — internal structures in relief
item.description: A second panorama of the same specimen with more pronounced relief. The outlines and spatial relationships of the internal organs are more clearly visible, especially the reproductive structures, intestinal ceca, and structures of the posterior body region.

item.title: Capsalid — whole mount
item.description: Panoramic whole-mount preparation of a capsalid monogenean. The pharynx, intestinal ceca, vitellaria, ovary, testes, and posterior attachment organ — the haptor — are clearly visible.

item.title: Chromatophores
item.description: Fragment of octopus skin. Chromatophores—pigment organs—are visible in different states, ranging from fully expanded (lighter, reddish-orange areas) to contracted (dark, dense spots).

item.title: Chromis
item.description: Scales of the fish Chromis viridis.

item.title: Chum salmon kidney — relatively preserved structure
item.description: Panoramic compression preparation of the kidney from a clinically healthy chum salmon after euthanasia. The renal tubules retain their usual structure and relatively clear lumina, while blood is distributed comparatively evenly throughout the tissue. The specimen serves as a control for comparison with pathological tubular changes.

item.title: Ciliated Epithelium of the Kidney
item.description: Ciliated epithelium within the renal tubules of a fish. The video shows ciliary motion in real time and then in slow motion, allowing the beating pattern to be observed in greater detail.

item.title: Ciliates and Bacteria on Fish Surfaces
item.description: The video shows free-living ciliates found on the surface of a fish together with bacterial aggregates among which they occur. Attention is often focused on the conspicuous and motile ciliates, whereas the bacterial component may remain unnoticed. Both native and stained preparations are presented to illustrate the spatial relationship between ciliates and bacteria. The footage demonstrates that the presence of ciliates alone does not explain the cause of a lesion and should be interpreted together with tissue condition and associated microbial communities.

item.title: Cocci
item.description: Coccoid bacteria.

item.title: Cryptobia Moving Through Detritus
item.description: The video shows flagellates of the genus Cryptobia actively moving between particles of detritus and mucus. Their characteristic locomotion, frequent changes in direction, and ability to pass through narrow spaces are clearly visible. Internal structures, including food vacuoles, can be observed in some individuals. The footage illustrates how these protozoans navigate through their natural microenvironment.

item.title: Cryptocaryon irritans in gills
item.description: Cryptocaryon irritans trophonts within the gill epithelium. The video demonstrates the gill-dominant form of cryptocaryoniasis, which may occur without the typical white spots on the skin.

item.title: Cryptosporidia 100x
item.description: Danio liver smear. May–Grünwald stain. Objective 100x.

item.title: Cryptosporidia 100x (ZN)
item.description: Danio liver smear. Ziehl–Neelsen stain. Objective 100x.

item.title: Degenerated Gills of a Dead Fish
item.description: Even markedly postmortem-altered gills may retain diagnostically relevant findings. Attached monogeneans can still be detected, helping to reveal potential parasitic threats and indicating what should be looked for in living fish.

item.title: Diagnostic Thinking
item.description: An interactive reasoning trainer: observations, conclusions, and the limits of evidence.

item.title: Discus
item.description: Scales of the fish Discus.

item.title: Division of Ichthyophthirius multifiliis
item.description: Palintomic division of a tomont after leaving the fish.

item.title: Erythrocytes
item.description: Erythrocytes showing signs of osmotic alteration.

item.title: Fibrous granulomas in gudgeon
item.description: Squash preparation of gudgeon (Gobio gobio) tissue. Multiple rounded structures of varying sizes with concentric arrangements of connective tissue fibers, consistent with fibrous granulomas.

item.title: Fin ray structure
item.description: A fin ray consists of two paired halves separated by living tissue. This video demonstrates fin ray anatomy and helps explain the mechanisms of fin erosion.

item.title: Fish necropsy
item.description: Fish necropsy with examination of internal organs and pathological findings.

item.title: Fungal Hyphae in Fish Tissues
item.description: Free spores alone do not prove tissue invasion. The video demonstrates the diagnostic sequence from external examination and hemorrhages to the detection of fungal hyphae actively growing within fish tissues.

item.title: Fungal structures
item.description: A preparation of mucus and contents from the empty stomach of a black ghost knifefish (Apteronotus albifrons). Numerous filamentous fungal structures are visible among mucus, detritus, and small rounded elements. This finding indicates a marked presence of fungal forms in the gastric lumen and is pathologically significant. Captured with a 40× objective.

item.title: Fungal Structures in a Native Preparation
item.description: Native preparation of fungal structures within fish tissue. The video shows hyphae, spores, and their arrangement without fixation, drying, or staining. This approach preserves the natural size and morphology of fungal elements, facilitating their recognition and comparison with stained preparations. The footage complements diagnostic materials on fungal lesions and demonstrates the appearance of spores and hyphae before artefacts associated with smear preparation are introduced.

item.title: Gadus
item.description: Scales of the fish Gadus.

item.title: Gills
item.description: Necrosis of gill lamellae.

item.title: Heart of an Amur Sleeper Larva Under the Microscope
item.description: The video shows the functioning heart of a rotan larva (Perccottus glenii). Due to the transparency of larval tissues, contractions of the atrium and ventricle, blood flow, and the operation of a two-chambered teleost heart can be observed directly. The footage illustrates basic aspects of fish circulation and provides a rare opportunity to observe cardiac activity without dissection or staining.

item.title: Hyphal and sporangial structures
item.description: A high-magnification May–Grünwald-stained preparation of intestinal contents. Hyphal structures and rounded sporangial forms are visible among mucus and fragments of food material. Together with the massive presence of yeast-like cells in the gastric contents, this finding indicates marked fungal involvement of the digestive tract. Captured with a 100× objective.

item.title: Ichthyobodo spp.: Comparing Morphotypes
item.description: The video compares two morphotypes of flagellates traditionally identified as Ichthyobodo spp. Differences in cell morphology and flagellar arrangement become apparent at high magnification. However, the available morphological features are insufficient for reliable species identification, and the taxonomic status of these forms remains uncertain.

item.title: Intracellular parasites 100x
item.description: Chrysiptera liver smear 100x. May–Grünwald stain. Parasites in histiocytes.

item.title: Labidochromis
item.description: Scales of the fish Labidochromis yellow.

item.title: Liver of Apteronotus albifrons with granulomatous lesions
item.description: A squash preparation from the intestine of Apteronotus albifrons. Multiple granulomatous lesions associated with a mycobacterial infection are visible among mucus and sloughed mucosal material. However, the etiology of such lesions cannot be determined from morphology alone without additional investigations.

item.title: Liver with lipid inclusions
item.description: A squash preparation of the liver of a neon tetra (Paracheirodon innesi). Numerous rounded lipid inclusions, uneven tissue coloration, and areas of marked blood filling are visible. This pattern reflects severe hepatic alteration and should be interpreted together with other findings. Captured with a 10× objective.

item.title: Loeffler vs Ziehl–Neelsen
item.description: The same smear is shown sequentially after Loeffler’s methylene blue stain and Ziehl–Neelsen staining. The video demonstrates how acid-fast bacteria become visible following a specialized staining procedure.

item.title: Microworms
item.description: Microworms in the brain membrane of a ray, 20x. Small nematodes.

item.title: Modified carbol fuchsin staining without acid decolorization
item.description: Intensely stained red-pink rod-shaped bacteria are visible in the tissue material against a contrasting background. Acid decolorization was not performed, so acid-fastness was not assessed. Try to find them all...

item.title: Monodactyl's Tail
item.description: The caudal fin of a Monodactylus. Note the soft tissue and ray segments.

item.title: Monodactylus
item.description: Scales of the fish Monodactylus.

item.title: Nematode eggs
item.description: Capillaria eggs from Danio intestine.

item.title: Pigment or Cocci?
item.description: Not every dark particle in a smear is a coccus. The same microscopic field is shown after staining and subsequent alcohol decolorization, illustrating the difference between bacterial structures and pigment granules.

item.title: Pigmented fungal structures on crab gills
item.description: Panorama fragment of crab gills showing branching septate hyphae and numerous pigmented rounded structures. Macroscopically, affected areas of the gills were black and showed tissue destruction.

item.title: Pleurogrammus
item.description: Scales of the fish Pleurogrammus.

item.title: Praziquantel in Water
item.description: Behavior of praziquantel after addition to water. Despite prior dissolution in alcohol, the compound forms a fine suspension and gradually settles. The video illustrates why the term "dispersion" is often more appropriate than "dissolution" in aquarium treatments.

item.title: Pterophyllum
item.description: Scales of the fish Pterophyllum scalare.

item.title: Renal concretions in neon tetra
item.description: Microscopic preparation of neon tetra kidney. Rounded and oval structures of varying sizes with distinct boundaries and heterogeneous contents, presumably mineral concretions. Some are surrounded by cellular structures resembling a granulomatous reaction. No mycobacteria were detected, and similar lesions were not observed in other organs.

item.title: Secret
item.description: What?

item.title: Thin fuchsin-positive bacteria
item.description: Impression smear. Ziehl–Neelsen staining. Numerous slender rod-shaped bacteria are observed among cellular elements. Morphological features alone do not allow identification at the genus level.

item.title: What 'many hexamitids' actually looks like
item.description: Dense aggregation of flagellated protozoans in a wet mount. The video demonstrates a parasite burden that is difficult to appreciate from still images alone.

item.title: Yeast-like structures
item.description: A May–Grünwald-stained preparation of gastric contents from a neon tetra (Paracheirodon innesi). Numerous rounded pink-purple structures with a clear capsule-like halo are visible. Morphologically, they are consistent with yeast-like fungal cells mixed with food material. Captured with a 40× objective.

item.title: Yellowtail kidney — tubular destruction
item.description: Panoramic compression preparation of yellowtail kidney. Areas with relatively preserved lighter tubular lumina can be compared with zones where the lumina are filled with dark material, corresponding to marked pathological change.
